claims.text: Minor Mo or W doping of near-equiatomic, low-noble-metal nanoparticles elevates the activation barrier for atomic diffusion.
An elevated diffusion activation barrier slows cation reordering and phase segregation during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operation.
Low refractory-element concentrations can be selected so as to avoid secondary-phase formation.
Incorporated refractory atoms enhance the diffusion barrier within the solid solution.
Refractory-element incorporation increases the activation energy for atomic diffusion and consequently reduces atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility limits cation reordering and phase segregation.
Limiting cation reordering and phase segregation preserves the metastable compositional uniformity of the nanoparticles under thermal stress.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, refractory-doped nanoparticles will show reduced grain-boundary movement and elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, refractory-doped nanoparticles will retain a more uniform phase during high-temperature exposure.
Undoped nanoparticles are expected to undergo appreciable atomic diffusion and phase segregation under the specified service regimes because they have lower diffusion activation barriers.
The proposed stabilizing effect is anticipated across catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric-relevant temperatures of 473–1923 K.
Excessive refractory-element concentration or secondary-phase formation may eliminate the beneficial stabilization effect or introduce undesirable properties.
Time-resolved grain-growth analysis can be used to estimate diffusion coefficients in these nanoparticles.

Failure of refractory-doped nanoparticles to show statistically significant reductions in grain growth, phase segregation, and elemental redistribution relative to an identically treated undoped control would falsify the proposed stabilization hypothesis.
